StepBack: Step-Level Error-Localized Resampling for Efficient Test-Time Reasoning

Yang Ouyang    Jung-Eun Kim ††thanks: Corresponding Author Affiliation: Department of Computer Science Affiliation: North Carolina State University Affiliation: {youyang7, jung-eun.kim}@ncsu.edu
Abstract

Self-consistency (SC) is a widely used decoding strategy for improving chain-of-thought reasoning, but it requires sampling many complete reasoning trajectories with a preset budget. Its efficient variants reduce the cost mainly by stopping full-trajectory sampling early or distributing the number of samples across questions. In this paper, we propose StepBack, a step-level error-localized resampling method for efficient test-time reasoning. Given a small set of draft trajectories, StepBack localizes likely first error positions using lightweight signals and then resamples the detected error step and its suffix, followed by majority answer voting. Empirically, StepBack matches the accuracy of SC on average across seven mathematical reasoning and multi-hop QA benchmarks, while reducing token usage by up to 41.26%. In addition, by nature, StepBack can be combined with adaptive inference methods such as Adaptive Consistency, further improving their inference-time efficiency. 11 1 Our code is available at: https://github.com/JEKimLab/StepBack

1 Introduction

Chain-of-thought prompting improves the reasoning ability of large language models (LLMs) (Brown et al., 2020) by encouraging language models to verbalize intermediate steps before producing a final answer (Wei et al., 2022; Kojima et al., 2022). A widely used approach to further improve accuracy is Self-Consistency (SC), which samples multiple “complete” reasoning trajectories and selects the most frequent final answer (Wang et al., 2022). Despite its effectiveness, SC is computationally expensive: each additional candidate answer requires generating an entire reasoning trajectory from scratch, so the token cost grows linearly with both the number of sampled trajectories and the length of each trajectory.

Recent studies have sought to reduce this cost by adjusting the number of full trajectories to sample. Adaptive-Consistency (AC) and Early-Stopping Self-Consistency (ESC) stop sampling once sufficient answer agreement is observed; Difficulty-Adaptive Self-Consistency (DSC) allocates larger budgets to harder questions; Reasoning-Aware Self-Consistency (RASC) makes stopping and voting more selective with rationale features (Aggarwal et al., 2023; Li et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025; Wan et al., 2025). These methods improve decisions on when to stop sampling or how many trajectories to sample, but they largely operate at the level of complete trajectories. As a result, they leave open a finer-grained question: where to efficiently spend additional sampling within a reasoning trajectory?

This question is important because reasoning failures often emerge at an intermediate reasoning step rather than at only the final answer (Wei et al., 2022; Uesato et al., 2022; Lightman et al., 2024). Once such an error occurs, subsequent steps may hinge on the corrupted reasoning state, causing the error to propagate and end up with an incorrect final answer, a phenomenon also noted in prior work on accumulated errors in chain-of-thought reasoning (Ling et al., 2023; Ouyang et al., 2026). Meanwhile, the early steps of a reasoning chain contain useful problem setup (Ji et al., 2025). This suggests a sensible opportunity for efficient test-time reasoning: if a likely first erroneous step can be localized, the valid early steps can be preserved while only the erroneous step and its subsequent suffixes are resampled (Tyen et al., 2024).

With this motivation, we propose StepBack, a step-level error-localized resampling method for efficient self-consistent reasoning. StepBack first generates a small set of draft trajectories and decomposes each trajectory into reasoning steps. It then uses lightweight signals, such as step-level negative log-likelihood, to localize likely first error positions. For each localized trajectory, StepBack reuses the earlier steps before the detected error, rolls back to the error step, and resamples the detected error step together with its suffixes. When no explicit error is detected, StepBack samples only the final answer step. The resulting candidate answers are then aggregated by majority voting, following the standard SC. This approach significantly cuts token usage while matching SC’s accuracy on average, as depicted in Figure 1. The key contributions of our work are:

Contributions.

  • •

    We introduce StepBack, an efficient step-level error-localized resampling method that reuses draft early steps, localizes likely first error positions with lightweight signals, and performs suffix resampling instead of repeated full-trajectory generation.

  • •

    To the best of our knowledge, StepBack is the first self-consistency-based decoding method that uses step-level error localization to decide where to begin resampling, rather than sampling every candidate as a full trajectory.

  • •

    We empirically show across mathematical reasoning and multi-hop QA benchmarks that StepBack can match or surpass full self-consistency while using substantially fewer generation tokens. We further show that StepBack can be seamlessly combined with adaptive inference methods such as Adaptive Consistency, Early-Stopping SC, and Difficulty-Adaptive SC.

2 Related Work

Efficient self-consistency.

Recent work reduces self-consistency cost by adaptively controlling the number of full trajectories to sample. Adaptive-Consistency stops once answer agreement is sufficient (Aggarwal et al., 2023); Early-Stopping Self-Consistency uses simple window-based stopping rules (Li et al., 2024); Reasoning-Aware Self-Consistency incorporates rationale-quality features into stopping and voting (Wan et al., 2025); and Difficulty-Adaptive Self-Consistency allocates larger budgets to harder questions (Wang et al., 2025). These methods improve sampling efficiency by deciding how many trajectories to generate. In contrast, StepBack solves the problem where additional computation should be spent inside a trajectory. Thus, StepBack is complementary to adaptive SC methods: they reduce the number of consumed candidates, while StepBack reduces the cost of each candidate.

Step-level signals and backtracking.

Process supervision and step-level verification show that intermediate reasoning steps carry useful signals about solution quality (Uesato et al., 2022; Lightman et al., 2024). Errors tend to propagate once an early step becomes invalid (Ling et al., 2023), early prefixes often contain reusable problem setup (Ji et al., 2025), and LLMs correct reasoning more effectively when the error location is given (Tyen et al., 2024). Several methods act on such signals by returning to an earlier step and regenerating from there: LeCo (Yao et al., 2024) restarts after the lowest-confidence step until two consecutive answers agree; Singh et al. (2025) backtrack with a step-level verifier conditioned on previously attempted revisions; Adaptive Rectification Sampling (Tan et al., 2025) prompts the model to rethink a step whose PRM score falls below a threshold; Thought Rollback (Chen and Li, 2024) rolls back to earlier thoughts after analyzing their errors; and Self-Backtracking (Yang et al., 2026) trains the model itself to decide when and where to backtrack. In these methods, each rollback depends on the outcome of earlier attempts, so revisions run sequentially and their total cost is not fixed in advance. StepBack instead uses lightweight signals, such as a negative log-likelihood increase or a process-reward score drop, to assign a single rollback point to each independent draft, so all suffix continuations can be generated in parallel and the number of candidate answers is fixed at B=nd​nsB=n_{d}n_{s}, the same budget as full-trajectory self-consistency. Each additional candidate reuses its draft prefix and therefore costs fewer tokens than a full trajectory, and StepBack requires no training and aggregates answers by standard majority voting.

3 Preliminaries and Motivating Observations

3.1 Step-Level Reasoning Trajectories

Let xx be an input problem and pθp_{\theta} be the language model. We write a reasoning trajectory as

τ=(z1,z2,…,zT,zT+1),\tau=(z_{1},z_{2},\ldots,z_{T},z_{T+1}), (1)

where z1,…,zTz_{1},\ldots,z_{T} are intermediate reasoning steps and zT+1z_{T+1} is the final-answer step. We denote the extracted answer by a⁡(τ)a(\tau).

Our method relies on the fact that instruction-tuned models usually produce naturally separable reasoning steps. For example, Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct often separates steps with blank lines, i.e., “\n\n”, in both math and multi-hop QA tasks. The other models we test show similar line-delimited outputs.

We therefore parse each trajectory into steps using blank-line boundaries. Examples of model outputs and the resulting step decomposition are provided in Appendix A.

3.2 The Value of Accurate Error Localization

For an incorrect trajectory, let e⁡(τ)e(\tau) denote the position of the first step where the reasoning becomes invalid.22 2 When there is no ambiguity, we omit (τ)(\tau). The earlier reasoning steps z<e⁡(τ)z_{<e(\tau)} remain valid, while the subsequent steps z≥e⁡(τ)z_{\geq e(\tau)} may be corrupted by the first error.

Draft–suffix resampling.

Given an answer budget BB, we consider a two-stage procedure shared by the oracle study below and by our method (Section 4). We first sample ndn_{d} draft trajectories τ(1),…,τ(nd)\tau^{(1)},\ldots,\tau^{(n_{d})}. For each draft τ(j)\tau^{(j)} with TjT_{j} reasoning steps, we choose a rollback point ej∈{1,…,Tj+1}e_{j}\in\{1,\ldots,T_{j}+1\}, keep the prefix z<ej(j)z^{(j)}_{<e_{j}}, and draw ns−1n_{s}-1 suffixes

z~ej:Tj+1(j)∼pθ(⋅∣x,z<ej(j)).\tilde{z}^{(j)}_{e_{j}:T_{j}+1}\sim p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x,z^{(j)}_{<e_{j}}). (2)

Together with the draft’s own answer, this yields B=nd​nsB=n_{d}n_{s} candidate answers, aggregated by majority vote as in self-consistency (SC). The only design choice is how to select eje_{j}.

Oracle rollback.

To understand the value of accurate error localization, we first consider an oracle setting where the true first-error position, e⁡(τ)e(\tau), is known, and set ej=e⁡(τ(j))e_{j}=e(\tau^{(j)}) for each draft. We obtain these oracle positions from first-error annotations produced by an LLM verifier prompt. We manually inspect 100 annotated samples and find no obvious misjudgments; the full annotation protocol and examples are provided in Appendix B and Appendix C. For drafts without an annotated first error, we set ej=Tj+1e_{j}=T_{j}+1 and resample only the final-step answer.

Table 1 reports motivating results under this oracle setting. Oracle first-error localization enables suffix resampling to match or even outperform full self-consistency while using fewer tokens. This suggests that many failed trajectories still contain useful early reasoning steps. Therefore, by reliably localizing the first errors and simply resampling from them, we can achieve both token efficiency and comparable (or better at times) accuracy.

4 StepBack: Step-Level Error-Localized Resampling

The oracle study in Section 3.2 shows that localized resampling can be effective when the first erroneous reasoning step is known. In practice, however, the true first-error position e⁡(τ)e(\tau) is unavailable at inference time. StepBack turns this oracle diagnostic into a practical decoding procedure by replacing e⁡(τ)e(\tau) with a predicted rollback point obtained from lightweight step-level signals.

For each draft τ(j)=(z1(j),…,zTj+1(j))\tau^{(j)}=(z^{(j)}_{1},\ldots,z^{(j)}_{T_{j}+1}), j=1,…,ndj=1,\ldots,n_{d}, StepBack applies an inference-time localization rule,

e^j=Loc⁡(x,τ(j))∈{1,…,Tj+1}.\hat{e}_{j}=\mathrm{Loc}(x,\tau^{(j)})\in\{1,\ldots,T_{j}+1\}. (3)

Here e^j≤Tj\hat{e}_{j}\leq T_{j} means that step e^j\hat{e}_{j} is predicted as the first unreliable reasoning step. StepBack then preserves the early steps (z1(j),…,ze^j−1(j))(z^{(j)}_{1},\ldots,z^{(j)}_{\hat{e}_{j}-1}) and resamples the detected step together with its suffix. If e^j=Tj+1\hat{e}_{j}=T_{j}+1, no explicit reasoning error is detected, so StepBack preserves the full reasoning chain and resamples only the final answer step to simply obtain the same number of answers as SC does. The resulting BB answer candidates are aggregated with the same normalized majority vote as done in SC. For details, see Algorithm 1.

4.1 Inference-Time Localization Signals

We instantiate Loc\mathrm{Loc} with lightweight inference-time signals in our experiments, including NLL-signal and PRM-signal. Throughout this subsection, we consider a single draft and omit the superscript (j)(j) (unless any confusion arises), writing τ=(z1,…,zT+1)\tau=(z_{1},\ldots,z_{T+1}).

NLL-signal: Step-Level Negative Log-Likelihood (NLL) Increase

For each reasoning step ztz_{t}, we compute its mean token negative log-likelihood under the base model:

ut=−1|zt|∑yi∈ztlogpθ(yi∣x,z<t,y<i).u_{t}=-\frac{1}{|z_{t}|}\sum_{y_{i}\in z_{t}}\log p_{\theta}\left(y_{i}\mid x,z_{<t},y_{<i}\right). (4)

A sudden increase in utu_{t} indicates that the model becomes less confident when generating the current step. We define

ΔtNLL=ut−ut−1,\Delta^{\mathrm{NLL}}_{t}=u_{t}-u_{t-1}, (5)

and predict the rollback point as

e^NLL={min⁡{t:ΔtNLL≥δNLL},if such a step exists,T+1,otherwise.\hat{e}_{\mathrm{NLL}}=\begin{cases}\min\{t:\Delta^{\mathrm{NLL}}_{t}\geq\delta_{\mathrm{NLL}}\},&\text{if such a step exists},\\ T+1,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (6)

The fallback position T+1T+1 means that no explicit reasoning error is detected. In this case, StepBack keeps the full reasoning chain and resamples only the final answer step.

PRM-signal: Step-Level Process Reward Model (PRM) Score Drop

We also consider an external process reward model (PRM), denoted by RϕR_{\phi}. Given the problem xx and the partial reasoning trace z≤tz_{\leq t}, the PRM assigns a score

rt=Rϕ​(x,z≤t),r_{t}=R_{\phi}(x,z_{\leq t}), (7)

which estimates the reliability of the reasoning prefix. A large drop after adding step ztz_{t} suggests that the new step makes the reasoning less reliable. We define

ΔtPRM=rt−1−rt,\Delta^{\mathrm{PRM}}_{t}=r_{t-1}-r_{t}, (8)

and predict the rollback point as

e^PRM={min⁡{t:ΔtPRM≥δPRM},if such a step exists,T+1,otherwise.\hat{e}_{\mathrm{PRM}}=\begin{cases}\min\{t:\Delta^{\mathrm{PRM}}_{t}\geq\delta_{\mathrm{PRM}}\},&\text{if such a step exists},\\ T+1,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (9)

In our experiments, unless otherwise specified, we use Qwen2.5-Math-PRM-7B (Zhang et al., 2025) as the PRM scorer.

Both signals are inexpensive. NLL-signal uses token probabilities already available from the base model, while the PRM-signal only scores partial reasoning traces rather than requiring additional full-trajectory sampling. We provide the detailed diagnostics in Appendix D.

4.2 Comparison with Self-Consistency

Standard self-consistency (SC) samples BB complete reasoning trajectories from pθ(⋅∣x)p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x) and returns the majority normalized answer (Wang et al., 2022). Under the same answer budget, SC spends all samples on independent full trajectories, whereas StepBack spends the budget on repairing or diversifying uncertain suffixes of a smaller set of draft anchors. This allows StepBack to reuse reliable early steps while focusing additional sampling on steps that are more likely to affect the final answer, as illustrated in Fig. 2.

5 Experiments

We evaluate whether StepBack can outperform or achieve a comparable performance to full-trajectory self-consistency (SC) at a fixed candidate-answer budget while reducing generation cost. The results focus on budget B=32B=32 and compare rollback-resampling against Greedy@1 and SC@32.

5.1 Experimental Setup

Benchmarks.

We evaluate mathematical reasoning on GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021), MATH500 (Hendrycks et al., 2021), AMC2023, AIME24, and OlympiadBench (He et al., 2024), covering tasks from grade-school arithmetic to competition-level mathematics. We further evaluate multi-hop question answering on HotpotQA (Yang et al., 2018) and 2WikiMultiHopQA (Ho et al., 2020), which require composing evidence across multiple supporting facts. For efficiency, we randomly sample 500 examples from the HotpotQA validation set of 7,405 examples and 1,000 examples from the 2WikiMultiHopQA validation set of 12.6K examples.

Models.

The model set contains Qwen-2.5-3B-Instruct, Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, and Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct. These models span various architectures and scales, allowing us to test whether error-localized suffix resampling is robust beyond a single backbone.

Baselines and variants.

The primary baseline is self-consistency (SC) (Wang et al., 2022), which samples B=32B=32 complete chain-of-thought trajectories independently and selects the most frequent normalized final answer. We also report greedy chain-of-thought decoding (CoT), which generates one deterministic reasoning trajectory and serves as a low-cost reference point. In Section 5.3, we additionally compare against adaptive reasoning methods, including Adaptive Consistency (AC) (Aggarwal et al., 2023), Early-Stopping Self-Consistency (ESC) (Li et al., 2024), and Difficulty-Adaptive Self-Consistency (DSC) (Wang et al., 2025). Details for their hyperparameters can be found in Appendix J. For the main comparison, StepBack uses the same candidate-answer budget as SC@32. We consider two lightweight variants of the localization signal: NLL-signal and PRM-signal, both described in Section 4.1.

Unless otherwise specified, we use thresholds 0.10.1 for NLL-signal and 0.050.05 for PRM-signal, without dataset-specific tuning. Lower thresholds trigger a rollback on modest drops of the step-level signal, so more drafts are rewritten since an earlier step; this favors accuracy over token saving. These thresholds are shared across all datasets and models; a held-out calibration on training questions (Appendix F) shows that every threshold in a wide grid matches or exceeds the average accuracy of SC@32 while saving 20–44% of tokens.

Evaluation metrics.

For all datasets, we report answer-level accuracy after answer extraction and normalization. For mathematical reasoning, extracted answers are compared against the reference answer using exact or symbolic equivalence when applicable. For multi-hop QA, we use normalized exact match. In Table 2, we report SC@32 accuracy once for each model-dataset pair and report StepBack by its accuracy change over SC,

Δ​Acc=Acc⁡(StepBack)−Acc⁡(SC​@​32),\Delta\mathrm{Acc}=\mathrm{Acc}(\textsc{StepBack})-\mathrm{Acc}(\mathrm{SC}@32), (10)

where positive values indicate that StepBack outperforms SC. We measure generation efficiency by the token saving relative to SC@32,

η=100​(1−Tok/Q⁡(StepBack)Tok/Q⁡(SC​@​32)),\eta=100\left(1-\frac{\mathrm{Tok/Q}(\textsc{StepBack})}{\mathrm{Tok/Q}(\mathrm{SC}@32)}\right), (11)

where Tok/Q\mathrm{Tok/Q} denotes the average number of generated tokens per question. In Table 3, we further report path expansion (PExp) (Jindal et al., 2026), the average number of sampled reasoning continuations per question, and

G/1​k​T=1000⋅Acc⁡(m)−Acc⁡(CoT)Tok/Q⁡(m),\mathrm{G/1kT}=1000\cdot\frac{\mathrm{Acc}(m)-\mathrm{Acc}(\mathrm{CoT})}{\mathrm{Tok/Q}(m)}, (12)

which measures the accuracy gain over greedy CoT per 1k generated tokens. Higher η\eta and G/1kT indicate better inference efficiency.

Implementation details.

Unless otherwise specified, we use temperature 0.70.7 and top-pp 0.950.95 for sampling. All experiments are run on compute nodes with two AMD EPYC 9005-series CPUs, and NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs (96 GB each); each run uses 4 GPUs with CUDA 12.8, PyTorch 2.7.0, and vLLM 0.9.2.

5.2 Main Results

Table 2 presents the main comparison between StepBack and SC@32 under the same candidate-answer budget B=32B=32. The main table reports the default StepBack configuration with nd=16n_{d}=16 draft trajectories and ns=2n_{s}=2 candidate answers per draft (the draft’s own answer and one localized suffix sample); additional budget allocations are reported in Section 6 and Appendix H. For each model–dataset pair, we report the SC@32 accuracy once, followed by the accuracy change Δ​Acc\Delta\mathrm{Acc}, token saving η\eta, and G/1kT of StepBack with PRM-signal and NLL-signal localization; the Avg. row gives the mean over the seven datasets weighted by their number of questions.

StepBack matches SC@32 accuracy on average with fewer generated tokens.

The Avg. rows of Table 2 summarize the comparison over all 4,166 questions. With PRM-signal, StepBack improves average accuracy over SC@32 by 0.360.36, 0.170.17, and 0.820.82 percentage points on Llama-3B, Qwen-3B and Qwen-7B, respectively, while generating 21.07%21.07\%, 18.66%18.66\%, and 22.80%22.80\% fewer tokens. With NLL-signal, it saves even more tokens, stays under 0.20.2 points difference with SC@32 on the two 3B models (+0.12+0.12 and −0.17-0.17), and is 0.550.55 points above SC@32 on Qwen-7B. Both signals also raise the accuracy gained per generated token: on Llama-3B, G/1kT increases from 1.392 for SC@32 to 1.769 with PRM-signal and 1.978 with NLL-signal.

Per dataset, PRM-signal reduces generated tokens in all 21 model–dataset pairs (7.66–41.26%), improves accuracy in 14 of them, ties in 1, and is lower in 6. On MATH500, it improves Qwen-3B, Llama-3B, and Qwen-7B by +0.40+0.40, +1.20+1.20, and +2.00+2.00 points while saving 25.60%25.60\%, 20.81%20.81\%, and 28.53%28.53\% tokens, respectively. Notably, although the PRM is trained primarily for mathematical process supervision, it also provides useful step-level reliability estimates for logical and multi-hop reasoning: on HotpotQA, PRM-signal improves Qwen-3B and Qwen-7B by +1.20+1.20 and +2.20+2.20 points but lowers Llama-3B by 2.002.00 points, which suggests that PRM-signal can capture some reasoning-quality drops beyond purely arithmetic errors, but less reliably than on mathematical reasoning.

Meanwhile, NLL-signal provides a complementary low-cost localization signal requiring no external model: it achieves larger token savings than PRM-signal on 17 of the 21 pairs and improves accuracy of Qwen-3B and Qwen-7B on two multi-hop QA datasets. We factor this in that NLL-signal tends to localize errors less aggressively, often rolling back closer to the final answer and therefore resampling shorter suffixes. This yields stronger token savings, but may leave more earlier reasoning errors unedited compared to PRM-signal.

Localization overhead is small relative to generation.

The additional cost of computing localization signals remains modest compared with the cost of generating complete reasoning trajectories. The relative localization overhead ρ16\rho_{16} in Table 2, i.e., the share of the wall-clock time of StepBack spent scoring the drafts, averages 8.38%8.38\%, 9.52%9.52\%, and 10.93%10.93\% for NLL-signal and 7.48%7.48\%, 9.86%9.86\%, and 6.98%6.98\% for PRM-signal on Llama-3B, Qwen-3B, and Qwen-7B, respectively. Thus, the token savings achieved by StepBack are not offset by a large scoring cost.

StepBack benefits from reusable early reasoning steps.

The gains of accuracy suggest that many incorrect draft trajectories are not entirely unhelpful since they often contain correct early steps. Instead of discarding these steps as SC does, StepBack keeps the reliable part of each draft and resamples only from the predicted error region. This design is especially effective on datasets where errors often arise in later reasoning stages, such as GSM8K, MATH500, and AMC2023, where PRM-signal improves accuracy for all three models while saving 10.83–41.26% of generated tokens. The consistent token reduction across all settings further indicates that localized resampling avoids a large amount of redundant early steps generation.

Limitations across harder datasets.

On harder competition-style benchmarks such as AIME24 and OlympiadBench, the gains are less stable, especially for Llama-3B. This suggests that some failures cannot be corrected by resampling only a localized suffix, since they may require revising earlier reasoning decisions or exploring a substantially different solution path.

Overall, these results support the central premise of StepBack: under a fixed answer budget, additional test-time compute can be spent more efficiently by resampling from a localized likely error step instead of regenerating every candidate from scratch.

5.3 StepBack as a Complement to Adaptive Reasoning

Table 3 shows that StepBack can be directly combined with adaptive reasoning methods. AC, ESC, and DSC originally operate on a pool of independently generated full trajectories and decide how many candidates to consume. We instead replace this full-trajectory pool with the StepBack suffix pool: StepBack first generates draft anchors and localized suffix continuations, and the adaptive policy is then applied to these suffix candidates. Therefore, StepBack reduces the token cost of each candidate, while AC/ESC/DSC further reduces the number of consumed candidates.

These two reductions compound. Relative to each adaptive method alone, adding StepBack cuts generated tokens by 22–24% on MATH500, 35–38% on GSM8K, and 6–7% on HotpotQA. Accuracy also improves in all six comparisons on GSM8K and HotpotQA, by 1.1–2.2 points, and G/1kT improves in all nine; on MATH500, accuracy is only 0.2–0.8 points lower. The most efficient combination, StepBack +DSC on GSM8K, uses 5.2×\times fewer tokens than SC@32 while being 0.9 points more accurate.

Overall, the combination improves the accuracy-cost trade-off over both standard SC and adaptive reasoning alone, showing that StepBack is a complementary intra-trajectory allocation strategy rather than a replacement for adaptive inference.

6 Analysis and Discussions

Different Process Reward Model Size.

Table 14 in Appendix H studies whether StepBack relies on a large PRM for error localization. We fix the generator to Qwen2.5-3B and evaluate on MATH500, comparing Skywork-o1-Open-PRM-Qwen-2.5-1.5B (He et al., 2025) with Qwen2.5-Math-PRM-7B under the same B=32B=32 candidate-answer budget.

The results show that StepBack does not require a PRM larger than the generator. With the 1.5B Skywork PRM, StepBack still outperforms SC@32 in the 8×48\times 4 setting, improving accuracy by +0.36+0.36 points while saving 23.8%23.8\% generation tokens, although the accuracy is 0.360.36 points below SC@32 at 16×216\times 2. The 7B Qwen PRM gives stronger localization and achieves a higher accuracy gain of +0.72+0.72 points at 16×216\times 2, but 1.5B PRM already preserves a substantial portion of the benefit with lower scoring overhead (13.7ms vs. 19.7ms per draft sample).

This suggests that the key requirement is not PRM scale, but whether the localization signal is informative. Even lightweight signals, such as NLL-signal or a smaller PRM, can support effective suffix resampling when they identify useful rollback points.

Drafts versus suffix samples.

Table 12 in Appendix H studies how to allocate the same candidate budget B=32B=32 between draft anchors and suffix samples. Suffix-heavy settings such as 1×321\times 32 and 2×162\times 16 save the most tokens and 2×162\times 16 attains the highest G/1kT on three out of the seven datasets, since many candidates share the same short early steps. However, they are less stable in accuracy because a small number of flawed draft prefixes can limit recovery.

Draft-heavy settings such as 8×48\times 4 and 16×216\times 2 are more robust because they provide more diverse reasoning prefixes. 8×48\times 4 improves over SC@32 on all five math benchmarks, and 16×216\times 2 improves on GSM8K, MATH500, AMC2023, AIME24, and HotpotQA and matches it on OlympiadBench, while still saving tokens. These exhibit that ndn_{d} and nsn_{s} control an accuracy-efficiency trade-off: suffix-heavy settings are more cost-oriented, whereas draft-heavy settings are more accuracy-oriented.

Alternative rollback rules.

Any rule that maps a draft to a rollback point can serve as Loc\mathrm{Loc} in Algorithm 1, including signal-free rules such as random, fixed-position, and final-step rollback, and PRM-based rules from prior backtracking methods (Singh et al., 2025; Tan et al., 2025). Appendix G compares them with drafting, suffix resampling, and majority voting held fixed. Prefix reuse and suffix resampling yield most of the token saving under any rule, and late rules such as final-step resampling are strong efficiency baselines; on HotpotQA, final-step resampling is both more accurate and cheaper than PRM-signal. Localization helps most when suffix samples dominate the vote: at 4×84\times 8, PRM-signal is 2.06 points more accurate than final-step resampling over all seven datasets.

7 Conclusion

We presented StepBack, a step-level error-localized resampling method for efficient test-time reasoning. Instead of regenerating every candidate from scratch, StepBack keeps the reliable prefix of each draft and resamples only from a likely first error located by lightweight NLL-signal or PRM-signal. Across seven mathematical reasoning and multi-hop QA benchmarks and three models, StepBack matches the average accuracy of SC@32 under the same answer budget while generating up to 41.26% fewer tokens, and it further reduces the cost of adaptive methods such as AC, ESC, and DSC. These results suggest that where test-time compute is spent within a trajectory is a useful axis of efficiency, complementary to deciding how many trajectories to sample.

8 Limitations and Broader Impact

Limitations.

StepBack has limitations that leave room for future work. First, we focus on two representative localization signals, NLL-signal and PRM-signal. Although they already show clear benefits, exploring a broader set of even lighter-weight signals may further improve the efficiency of StepBack. Second, our experiments mainly focus on mathematical reasoning and multi-hop question answering. While StepBack performs well in these settings, its generalizability to other domains such as code generation or long-context summarization remains to be further studied.

Broader impact.

More efficient reasoning can make stronger inferences accessible at a lower cost, which is a positive outcome for scientific and educational use. At the same time, cheaper reasoning can also make capable systems easier to deploy at scale. We therefore believe that research on efficient reasoning should ideally improve both performance and transparency about where the gains come from.

Appendix

Appendix A Step Decomposition Examples

Our method assumes that model outputs can be decomposed into reasoning steps. In practice, the tested instruction-tuned models usually produce line-delimited or numbered reasoning.

For Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, steps are often separated by blank lines, i.e., “\n\n”, and frequently begin with explicit numbers such as “1.”, “2.”, etc. We use these boundaries to parse trajectories into steps.

A.1 GSM8K Example

The following is a representative Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct output on GSM8K.

Sure, let’s break down the problem step by step.

1. Determine the total number of eggs laid per day:
Janet’s ducks lay 16 eggs per day.

2. Calculate the number of eggs eaten for breakfast:
Janet eats 3 eggs for breakfast each morning.

3. Calculate the number of eggs used for baking muffins:
Janet uses 4 eggs to bake muffins for her friends.

4. Calculate the total number of eggs used:
3+4=73+4=7.

5. Calculate the number of eggs remaining:
16−7=916-7=9.

6. Determine the revenue:
9×2=189\times 2=18.

So, Janet makes 18\boxed{18} dollars every day at the farmers’ market.

This output is naturally segmented into six reasoning steps plus the final answer. The blank-line and numbered-step structure makes the parsing deterministic.

A.2 Multi-hop QA Example

The same behavior appears in general QA tasks. For example, on a HotpotQA-style multihop question, Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct produces:

Let’s break down the question and answer it step by step:

1. Identify the key information: The question is about Curt Menefee, Michael Anthony Strahan, and their NFL show.

2. Determine the Fox network’s NFL show: The Fox network has a show featuring Curt Menefee and Michael Anthony Strahan, called “Fox NFL Sunday.”

3. Identify the co-host: Michael Anthony Strahan is one of the co-hosts of this show.

4. Find the team with which Strahan spent his entire 15-year career: Michael Anthony Strahan played for the New York Giants.

5. Conclusion: The team is the New York Giants.

The answer is: The New York Giants.

We apply the same segmentation rule across datasets and models. The final answer sentence is treated as an additional special step.

Appendix B Oracle First-Error Annotation Protocol

For diagnostic analysis, we construct reference first-error annotations using GPT-5.1 as an external verifier. Given an incorrect model-generated trajectory, we prompt GPT-5.1 to identify the earliest step that contains a clear arithmetic, formula, or reasoning error. These annotations are used only for oracle and diagnostic experiments, not for training or tuning StepBack.

The following prompt is used for GSM8K-style math problems.

You are a rigorous math reasoning verifier.

Question:
{question}

Correct final answer: {gold_answer}

The model produced the following step-by-step solution
(which arrives at a WRONG final answer):

{numbered_steps}

Judgment criteria (follow strictly):
- Focus ONLY on mathematical operations. For each step, check whether the
  arithmetic (addition, subtraction, multiplication, percentages, etc.) is
  performed correctly on the numbers it uses.
- A step is CORRECT if: (a) its arithmetic is right, AND (b) the numbers it
  uses come from the problem statement or from a preceding step’s result.
  It does not matter what the step calls or labels the result.
- A step is INCORRECT only if: (a) it computes an arithmetic operation wrong
  (e.g. 2+3=6), OR (b) it applies a formula/percentage to a number that
  neither the problem statement nor any preceding step provided as the
  appropriate base for that operation.
- Steps that merely restate the problem, outline a plan, set up notation,
  or compute simple sums of previously stated numbers are correct even if
  the label/name they give the result is imprecise.
- Do NOT mark a step wrong for imprecise wording or naming.
- Do NOT mark a step wrong just because it propagates an earlier mistake.

Task:
1. Walk through every step. For each, decide correct/incorrect by the
   criteria above.
2. If you find an incorrect step, report the FIRST one and explain in one
   sentence what error it introduces.
3. If NO step contains a clear arithmetic or formula error by the criteria
   above, set first_error_step to -1.

Output STRICT JSON:
{
  "first_error_step": <int, 1-indexed; or -1 if no clear error found>,
  "total_steps": {len(steps)},
  "reason": "<one sentence explaining the error, or ’no clear error found’>"
}

We applied this verifier to all 16 sampled drafts per question for Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct on GSM8K and MATH500. To assess annotation quality, we manually inspected 100 randomly sampled annotations and found no obvious misjudgments under the stated criteria. We therefore use these annotations as oracle first-error labels for diagnostic experiments. We emphasize that these labels are used only for analysis and oracle studies; the proposed test-time method does not require GPT-5.1 annotations.

Appendix D First-Error Localization Diagnostics

In this section, we evaluate whether lightweight signals can approximate the oracle first-error positions used in Section 3.2. For each incorrect trajectory, we have an annotated first-error position ee. Given a localization signal, we predict a first-error position e^\hat{e} and compare it against ee. We also include a baseline, Random, that samples a rollback position randomly from the available reasoning steps in the trajectory. This baseline tests whether the signal-based methods do better than selecting a resampling point without using any information from the trajectory.

For each trajectory with annotated first-error position ee, we evaluate the predicted position e^\hat{e} using the following four metrics.

I. Exact.

Exact measures whether the predicted position exactly matches the annotated first-error step:

e^=e.\hat{e}=e. (13)

II. Prev-1.

Prev-1 measures whether the predicted position is either the annotated first-error step or the immediately preceding step:

e^∈{max⁡(1,e−1),e}.\hat{e}\in\{\max(1,e-1),e\}. (14)

This metric captures whether the predicted resampling point is close enough to cover the first error while avoiding substantial wasted computation on already-correct early reasoning steps. When e^=e\hat{e}=e, resampling starts exactly at the first error; when e^=e−1\hat{e}=e-1, only one additional valid step is resampled.

III. Not-Later.

Not-Later measures whether the predicted position occurs before or exactly at the first error:

e^≤e.\hat{e}\leq e. (15)

This metric is important because resampling from a position before or at the true first error includes the erroneous step in the resampled suffix. However, it should be interpreted together with pre-error distance: a very early prediction can satisfy Not-Later while wasting computation by resampling many already-correct early reasoning steps. Hence, we also introduce the following metric.

IV. Mean Pre-Error Distance.

Mean Pre-Error Distance measures how far the predicted position is before the annotated first-error step, counting only predictions that occur before or at the true first error:

e−e^for trajectories with ​e^≤e.e-\hat{e}\quad\text{for trajectories with }\hat{e}\leq e. (16)

A lower value indicates that the predicted resampling point is closer to the first error while still covering it. This metric distinguishes useful early localization from overly conservative (i.e., too late) predictions that restart too much of the reasoning trajectory.

Discussion.

Table 5 shows that both lightweight signals contain information about where reasoning first becomes unreliable. PRM-signal with a threshold of δ=\delta=0.05 achieves the best Exact and Prev-1 scores. For the same threshold, 52.3%52.3\% Not-Later rate indicates that the predicted point often falls no later than the annotated first-error step, making it possible to rewrite the erroneous step itself. Meanwhile, its Mean Pre-Error Distance remains at only 1.071.07, explaining that it typically wastes about one correct step on average. This shows that an external process-level scorer can identify local reasoning degradation more accurately and place the resampling point close to the oracle first error without excessive early resampling. NLL-signal is weaker than PRM-signal, but still outperforms the Random baseline in all metrics except for Not-Later, exhibiting that sudden increases in token-level uncertainty may also provide a meaningful, though less precise, signal of reasoning failure.

Appendix E Full Oracle Error-Localized Resampling Results

Table 6 reports the full oracle error-localized resampling sweep. In this oracle setting, resampling starts from the annotated first-error position. When no clear first error is annotated, we fall back to resampling from the final-answer step. Here, ndn_{d} denotes the number of draft trajectories, and nsn_{s} denotes the number of candidate answers obtained from each draft.

These results provide additional evidence for the motivating observation in Section 3.2: if the first error can be accurately localized, suffix resampling can reuse useful early reasoning steps, reduce token usage, and achieve comparable or even better accuracy than full self-consistency.

Appendix F Threshold Calibration on Held-out Data

The main experiments use a single threshold per signal for all datasets and models, δNLL=0.1\delta_{\mathrm{NLL}}=0.1 and δPRM=0.05\delta_{\mathrm{PRM}}=0.05. To examine how sensitive StepBack is to this choice, we calibrate both thresholds on held-out training questions.

Protocol.

We sample 100 questions from the MATH training set [Hendrycks et al., 2021] and 100 from the HotpotQA training set [Yang et al., 2018]. We run StepBack with Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct in the 16×216\times 2 setting under two random seeds and sweep each threshold over the grid in Table 7. Each threshold is scored by the macro average of MATH and HotpotQA accuracy, and the highest-scoring threshold is selected, with ties broken in favor of fewer generated tokens.

Results.

Table 7 shows that StepBack is robust to the threshold: every value in the grid matches or exceeds the macro score of SC@32 (62.00) while saving 19.67–44.37% of generated tokens. Larger thresholds flag fewer steps, so more drafts keep their full reasoning chain and resample only the final answer step (Section 4.1); token savings therefore increase monotonically with δ\delta. As δ\delta increases, HotpotQA accuracy tends to increase, while MATH accuracy stays within 1.5 points of SC@32.

The calibration selects δNLL=0.5\delta_{\mathrm{NLL}}=0.5 and δPRM=0.8\delta_{\mathrm{PRM}}=0.8, both larger than our defaults. On this held-out set, the defaults match MATH accuracy at the SC@32 level (80.00) and save 25.25% and 21.43% of tokens, whereas the selected thresholds save 42.58% and 38.92% with a higher macro score. Our defaults thus sit at the low-saving end of the grid rather than at the calibrated optimum, which suggests that the gains in Section 5.2 do not rely on a favorable choice of δ\delta.

Appendix G Comparison with Alternative Rollback Rules

The framework of StepBack does not fix how the rollback point is chosen. For a given allocation (nd,ns)(n_{d},n_{s}), drafting, suffix resampling, and majority voting are consistent across rules, and only the localization rule Loc\mathrm{Loc} of Section 4 changes. This lets us separate the effect of localization from the effect of reusing prefixes and resampling suffixes. All results in this section use Qwen-3B, the sampling settings of Section 5.1, and B=32B=32 answers per question.

Signal-free rules.

These rules ignore the content of the draft. Random rolls back to a step drawn uniformly at random from the draft’s reasoning steps, as in Table 5. Fixed-qq rolls back to the step at a fixed fraction q∈{25%,50%,75%}q\in\{25\%,50\%,75\%\} of the draft’s reasoning steps. Final-step sets e^j=Tj+1\hat{e}_{j}=T_{j}+1 for every draft: it keeps the whole reasoning chain and resamples only the final-answer step. This is also the fallback of NLL-signal and PRM-signal when no step crosses the threshold, so both signals approach Final-step as δ\delta grows.

Rules inspired by prior backtracking methods.

Several test-time methods revise a reasoning trace from a step flagged as erroneous. We keep only their rule for choosing that step, compute it with the same PRM as PRM-signal (Qwen2.5-Math-PRM-7B), and leave the rest of StepBack unchanged.

  • •

    Min-advantage is inspired by Singh et al. [2025]. The original method identifies backtracking points based on changes in a process verifier’s predictions and performs multiple rounds of revision using a verifier conditioned on previous attempts. Our version rolls back to the step with the most negative advantage rt−rt−1r_{t}-r_{t-1}, i.e., e^j=arg⁡maxt⁡ΔtPRM\hat{e}_{j}=\arg\max_{t}\Delta^{\mathrm{PRM}}_{t}. Unlike PRM-signal, it rolls back in every draft, however small the largest drop is.

  • •

    Absolute-PRM is inspired by AR-Sampling [Tan et al., 2025]. AR-Sampling scores each step with a PRM during generation. When the score falls below a fixed threshold, it keeps the step and appends a trigger sentence asking the model to rethink from that step. Our version rolls back to the first step whose PRM score is below 0.80.8, i.e., e^j=min⁡{t:rt<0.8}\hat{e}_{j}=\min\{t:r_{t}<0.8\}, and otherwise falls back to Tj+1T_{j}+1. It replaces the relative score drop of PRM-signal with an absolute score threshold.

Results over all seven datasets.

Table 8 compares all rules at (nd,ns)=(16,2)(n_{d},n_{s})=(16,2) over the 4,166 questions of Table 2. First, every rule saves tokens relative to SC@32 (5.29–44.07%) while staying within 0.25 points of its accuracy. This suggests that much of the token saving in StepBack comes from reusing prefixes and resampling suffixes, regardless of the rollback rule. Second, rules that roll back late are strong efficiency baselines: Fixed-75% and Final-step are 0.05 points above SC@32 while saving 33.66% and 44.07% of tokens. Compared with Final-step, NLL-signal and PRM-signal improve accuracy by only 0.07 and 0.12 percentage points, respectively. Their token-saving rates are 19.51 and 27.11 percentage points lower, respectively. Third, the two signals reach the highest accuracy among all rules. NLL-signal is above Random, Fixed-25%, Fixed-50%, Min-advantage, and Absolute-PRM on both accuracy and saving. Among the PRM-based rules, PRM-signal is above Min-advantage on both axes (+0.41+0.41 points of accuracy and +1.15+1.15 points of saving), and it is 0.12 points more accurate than Absolute-PRM while saving 0.93 points fewer tokens. Unlike Min-advantage, PRM-signal rolls back only when the score drop reaches δ\delta, so drafts without a clear failure keep their whole reasoning chain.

Five-seed results on MATH500 and HotpotQA.

Table 9 repeats the comparison over five seeds for all three allocations. On MATH500, PRM-signal with the 7B PRM has the highest mean accuracy at every allocation (tied with the 1.5B PRM at 8×\times4). It exceeds the best signal-free rule by 0.88–0.96 percentage points. At each allocation, this gap exceeds the seed standard deviation of either method. The most accurate signal-free rule, Fixed-25%, saves only 6.4–11.0% of tokens. With the 1.5B PRM, PRM-signal is also above every signal-free rule at 4×\times8 and 8×\times4. NLL-signal is less accurate than most signal-free rules on MATH500, consistent with its weaker localization in Table 5.

On HotpotQA, Final-step is the most accurate rule at every allocation and also saves the most tokens, so neither signal improves on it for this task. Among the remaining rules, NLL-signal is the most accurate at 4×\times8, while PRM-signal with the 1.5B PRM is the most accurate at 8×\times4 and 16×\times2. With the math-specific 7B PRM, however, PRM-signal is less accurate than Random at 4×\times8 and 8×\times4. The strong performance of Final-step cannot be explained by its 16 drafts alone. SC@16 is 1.4 and 1.2 percentage points below SC@32 on MATH500 and HotpotQA, respectively. In contrast, Final-step at 16×\times2 is only 0.80 percentage points below SC@32 on MATH500 and 2.20 percentage points above it on HotpotQA.

When localization matters.

Table 10 compares Final-step with both signals at every allocation over all seven datasets. The accuracy advantage of localization shrinks as draft answers account for a larger share of the 32 votes: PRM-signal is 2.06, 0.56, and 0.12 points more accurate than Final-step at 4×\times8, 8×\times4, and 16×\times2, and NLL-signal is 0.70, 0.24, and 0.07 points more accurate. Final-step saves more tokens in every case.

The final vote explains this trend. Each draft contributes its original answer and ns−1n_{s}-1 answers from rewritten suffixes. Thus, original draft answers contribute ndn_{d} of the 32 votes, and rewritten answers contribute the remaining nd​(ns−1)n_{d}(n_{s}-1). Localization changes only the rewritten answers. Let VDV_{D}, VRV_{R}, and VfullV_{\mathrm{full}} denote the most frequent answer (the mode, which need not hold a majority) among the draft answers, the rewrite answers, and all 32 answers, respectively. We call a question a conflict when VD≠VRV_{D}\neq V_{R}. Over the 4,166 questions, StepBack with PRM-signal has 1,098, 853, and 756 conflicts at 4×\times8, 8×\times4, and 16×\times2 (Table 11). The final answer VfullV_{\mathrm{full}} matches VRV_{R} in 89.34%, 74.33%, and 48.02% of these conflicts, respectively. It matches VDV_{D} in 6.92%, 19.58%, and 43.39%, respectively. In the remaining conflicts, the final answer matches neither. When rewrites contribute 28 of the 32 votes, their most frequent answer wins almost all conflicts. When drafts and rewrites contribute 16 votes each, this share falls to about half. Based on these observations, we can draw that localization determines where suffix rewriting starts, and the allocation determines how much the rewritten answers influence the final vote.

Raising the threshold moves both signals toward Final-step, because more drafts fall back to resampling only the final-answer step. The last two rows of Table 10 use δNLL=0.5\delta_{\mathrm{NLL}}=0.5 and δPRM=0.8\delta_{\mathrm{PRM}}=0.8. With δPRM=0.8\delta_{\mathrm{PRM}}=0.8, PRM-signal saves 36.76–64.53% of tokens and is still 1.68, 1.06, and 0.19 points more accurate than Final-step. At 8×\times4 and 16×\times2, it is also 0.58 and 0.24 percentage points more accurate than SC@32, respectively. It also achieves higher accuracy and greater token savings than PRM-signal with δPRM=0.05\delta_{\mathrm{PRM}}=0.05. With δNLL=0.5\delta_{\mathrm{NLL}}=0.5, the token-saving rate of NLL-signal is only 2.74–4.81 percentage points lower than that of Final-step. Its accuracy matches Final-step at 4×\times8 and is lower at the other two allocations, consistent with its weaker localization.

Summary.

Within StepBack, the rollback rule sets an accuracy–efficiency trade-off rather than having a single best choice. Signal-free late rollback, especially Final-step, gives the largest savings and is the most accurate rule on HotpotQA. Localization signals give the highest pooled accuracy, and with a 7B PRM, the highest MATH500 accuracy, and their benefit is largest when rewritten suffixes dominate the vote. The threshold δ\delta moves each signal along this trade-off, from early rollback toward the Final-step fallback.

Appendix J Hyperparameter Settings

Early-Stopping Methods.

We combine StepBack with three early-stopping criteria from the self-consistency literature:

  • •

    AC (Adaptive Consistency): Stops sampling when the Beta posterior confidence that the current plurality answer is correct exceeds θac=0.99\theta_{\text{ac}}=0.99.

  • •

    ESC (Early Stopping Consistency): Stops when all answers within a sliding window of size w=5w=5 are unanimous.

  • •

    DSC (Difficulty-Adaptive Self-Consistency): Uses a Beta posterior with confidence threshold θdsc=0.95\theta_{\text{dsc}}=0.95 for easy questions and a hard-question threshold of 0.500.50; stops early when confidence is reached or abandons when confidence remains low after half the budget is consumed.

Appendix K Random-Seed Robustness

Table 16 reports random-seed robustness on MATH500 across five seeds. PRM 8×\times4 and PRM 16×\times2 improve over SC@32, raising the mean accuracy from 72.84%72.84\% to 73.20%73.20\% and 73.56%73.56\%, with mean paired gains of +0.36+0.36 and +0.72+0.72 points, while PRM 4×\times8 is 0.440.44 points lower. Both 8×\times4 and 16×\times2 outperform SC@32 in 4 out of 5 seeds; on the remaining seed, 8×\times4 is 0.20.2 points lower and 16×\times2 ties. The gains are therefore small, but they are not caused by a single favorable seed.

NeurIPS Paper Checklist

  1. 1.

    Claims

  2. Question: Do the main claims made in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the paper’s contributions and scope?

  3. Answer: [Yes]

  4. Justification: The abstract and introduction summarize the main contribution of StepBack as an error-localized suffix resampling method for efficient test-time reasoning.

  5. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the abstract and introduction do not include the claims made in the paper.

    • •

      The abstract and/or introduction should clearly state the claims made, including the contributions made in the paper and important assumptions and limitations. A [No] or [N/A] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers.

    • •

      The claims made should match theoretical and experimental results, and reflect how much the results can be expected to generalize to other settings.

    • •

      It is fine to include aspirational goals as motivation as long as it is clear that these goals are not attained by the paper.

  6. 2.

    Limitations

  7. Question: Does the paper discuss the limitations of the work performed by the authors?

  8. Answer: [Yes]

  9. Justification: We discuss limitations in Section 8.

  10. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper has no limitation while the answer [No] means that the paper has limitations, but those are not discussed in the paper.

    • •

      The authors are encouraged to create a separate “Limitations” section in their paper.

    • •

      The paper should point out any strong assumptions and how robust the results are to violations of these assumptions (e.g., independence assumptions, noiseless settings, model well-specification, asymptotic approximations only holding locally). The authors should reflect on how these assumptions might be violated in practice and what the implications would be.

    • •

      The authors should reflect on the scope of the claims made, e.g., if the approach was only tested on a few datasets or with a few runs. In general, empirical results often depend on implicit assumptions, which should be articulated.

    • •

      The authors should reflect on the factors that influence the performance of the approach. For example, a facial recognition algorithm may perform poorly when image resolution is low or images are taken in low lighting. Or a speech-to-text system might not be used reliably to provide closed captions for online lectures because it fails to handle technical jargon.

    • •

      The authors should discuss the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithms and how they scale with dataset size.

    • •

      If applicable, the authors should discuss possible limitations of their approach to address problems of privacy and fairness.

    • •

      While the authors might fear that complete honesty about limitations might be used by reviewers as grounds for rejection, a worse outcome might be that reviewers discover limitations that aren’t acknowledged in the paper. The authors should use their best judgment and recognize that individual actions in favor of transparency play an important role in developing norms that preserve the integrity of the community. Reviewers will be specifically instructed to not penalize honesty concerning limitations.

  11. 3.

    Theory assumptions and proofs

  12. Question: For each theoretical result, does the paper provide the full set of assumptions and a complete (and correct) proof?

  13. Answer: [N/A]

  14. Justification: The paper does not present formal theoretical results such as theorems or lemmas. We include only analytical discussions to provide intuition for the proposed method.

  15. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include theoretical results.

    • •

      All the theorems, formulas, and proofs in the paper should be numbered and cross-referenced.

    • •

      All assumptions should be clearly stated or referenced in the statement of any theorems.

    • •

      The proofs can either appear in the main paper or the supplemental material, but if they appear in the supplemental material, the authors are encouraged to provide a short proof sketch to provide intuition.

    • •

      Inversely, any informal proof provided in the core of the paper should be complemented by formal proofs provided in appendix or supplemental material.

    • •

      Theorems and Lemmas that the proof relies upon should be properly referenced.

  16. 4.

    Experimental result reproducibility

  17. Question: Does the paper fully disclose all the information needed to reproduce the main experimental results of the paper to the extent that it affects the main claims and/or conclusions of the paper (regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not)?

  18. Answer: [Yes]

  19. Justification: Section 5 describes the evaluated datasets, models, decoding hyperparameters, sample budgets, voting procedure, and evaluation metrics needed to reproduce the main results.

  20. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

    • •

      If the paper includes experiments, a [No] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers: Making the paper reproducible is important, regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not.

    • •

      If the contribution is a dataset and/or model, the authors should describe the steps taken to make their results reproducible or verifiable.

    • •

      Depending on the contribution, reproducibility can be accomplished in various ways. For example, if the contribution is a novel architecture, describing the architecture fully might suffice, or if the contribution is a specific model and empirical evaluation, it may be necessary to either make it possible for others to replicate the model with the same dataset, or provide access to the model. In general. releasing code and data is often one good way to accomplish this, but reproducibility can also be provided via detailed instructions for how to replicate the results, access to a hosted model (e.g., in the case of a large language model), releasing of a model checkpoint, or other means that are appropriate to the research performed.

    • •

      While NeurIPS does not require releasing code, the conference does require all submissions to provide some reasonable avenue for reproducibility, which may depend on the nature of the contribution. For example

      1. (a)

        If the contribution is primarily a new algorithm, the paper should make it clear how to reproduce that algorithm.

      2. (b)

        If the contribution is primarily a new model architecture, the paper should describe the architecture clearly and fully.

      3. (c)

        If the contribution is a new model (e.g., a large language model), then there should either be a way to access this model for reproducing the results or a way to reproduce the model (e.g., with an open-source dataset or instructions for how to construct the dataset).

      4. (d)

        We recognize that reproducibility may be tricky in some cases, in which case authors are welcome to describe the particular way they provide for reproducibility. In the case of closed-source models, it may be that access to the model is limited in some way (e.g., to registered users), but it should be possible for other researchers to have some path to reproducing or verifying the results.

StepBack may improve the efficiency and accessibility of reasoning-time inference, but stronger reasoning systems can also be misused or produce more persuasive incorrect outputs; we therefore emphasize careful evaluation and deployment.

For example, it is legitimate to point out that an improvement in the quality of generative models could be used to generate Deepfakes for disinformation.
